text:
The taste of sugar is deceptive; it is a sharp, crystalline sweetness that dissolves instantly on the tongue, leaving behind a hollow, sticky residue that lingers long after the initial pleasure fades. It is the flavor of immediate gratification masking a slow decay.

Liam stood before the canvas, the smell of turpentine and linseed oil thick in the air, but his mind was elsewhere, trapped in the suffocating warmth of his father’s study. The conflict was no longer just a choice between two careers; it was a battle for his very soul. His father, a man whose hands were calloused from decades of honest labor in the family’s textile mill, had laid down the law with a finality that shook the house: "Art does not pay the bills, Liam. It does not keep the lights on. You will take your place at the loom, or you will take your place in the gutter."

The pressure mounted not with a shout, but with a silent, crushing weight. Every brushstroke Liam made felt like a betrayal, a theft of time that belonged to the family legacy. Yet, every time he tried to pick up a shuttle, his hands trembled, and the vision of color in his mind turned to gray ash. The rift between them was no longer just a disagreement; it was a chasm. His father’s disappointment was a physical presence, a cold draft that seeped into the rooms where Liam tried to create. And Liam’s resentment was a poison, souring every meal, every conversation, turning the home into a battlefield where silence was the loudest weapon. He was torn apart, not by the desire to choose, but by the terrifying realization that choosing either path meant destroying the other. The sugar of his ambition was sweet, but the cost was becoming bitter enough to choke on.
